channel.title: Longhand | The Dry Text Co.
channel.description: Writing about writing, from a content agency in Ahmedabad. A new piece most mornings.

item.title: Following up on a quote after the silence, without sounding desperate
item.description: The quote went out and the client went quiet. How to follow up with something they can actually reply to.

item.title: Writing an apology to a customer when you got it wrong
item.description: Most business apologies regret the inconvenience and skip the mistake. How to write one that names it.

item.title: Naming your service packages so customers can tell them apart
item.description: Silver, Gold and Platinum only tell a customer the price order. How to name packages that explain themselves.

item.title: Writing a Reel script: the first two seconds, and what to say in the rest
item.description: Most Reels are scrolled past before the logo appears. How to write the first two seconds, and the rest.

item.title: The line under your name on LinkedIn: what a founder's headline should say
item.description: The line under your name is read more than any post. What a founder's headline should say.

item.title: The service page: what to put on it when everyone offers the same service
item.description: Everyone lists the same services with the same bullets. What to write on yours so a buyer can tell you apart.

item.title: Replying to Google reviews, the kind ones and the angry ones
item.description: A reply to a review is read by the next customer more than the last. How to write the kind and angry ones.

item.title: The WhatsApp away message, and quick replies that don't sound like a machine
item.description: Written once, sent for years. How to write the away message, the greeting and the quick replies.

item.title: The back of the pack: what to write after the ingredients
item.description: After the legal declarations, a small panel is left on the pack. What to write in it.

item.title: Writing an event invitation people actually turn up to
item.description: Most invitations get a thumbs up and an empty chair. How to write one people turn up to.

item.title: A company profile for a tender, without the mission statement
item.description: A tender profile is read by a committee with a checklist. Write it for the checklist.

item.title: The menu is copy: writing a cafe or restaurant menu people order from
item.description: Every customer reads the menu in full, just before they pay. How to write one people order from.

item.title: The small words on a website: buttons, error messages, empty states
item.description: Buttons, error messages and empty pages are written last and read at the moment people decide to leave.

item.title: Writing for doctors, lawyers and CAs without sounding like a pamphlet
item.description: Most professional websites list everything and explain nothing. How to write for the worried reader.

item.title: Brochures: does anyone read them, and what to put in the one they do
item.description: Most brochures go in a drawer. The one that gets read is read by someone who wasn't in the meeting.

item.title: Should your website show prices?
item.description: Price on request feels safe and reads as expensive. When to show the number, and how to write it.

item.title: Writing a price increase message customers don't leave over
item.description: Most price increase messages apologise for a paragraph and hide the number. Put the number first.

item.title: Writing a case study when the client won't let you name them
item.description: The client said no to the logo, so the case study never got written. How to write one that works without a name.

item.title: How to write a job post that good people answer
item.description: Most job posts read like a notice, so the good people scroll past. What to write instead.

item.title: The Contact page: the last page before money, and the least written
item.description: The page where a visitor decides to spend money is usually a form and a map. What to write there instead.

item.title: Why every Diwali post looks the same, and how to write one that doesn't
item.description: Diya, rangoli, prosperity in gold. How to write the Diwali post only your business could send.

item.title: Writing a hoarding: seven words at sixty kilometres an hour
item.description: A hoarding gets one glance from someone driving at sixty. Seven words is plenty. Here is what to cut.

item.title: Email subject lines that get opened without lying
item.description: Fake Re:, false Urgent, a quick question that isn't. How to get the open without the small lie.

item.title: How many revisions a writer should include, and what counts as one
item.description: Two rounds of revisions means nothing until someone says what a round is. How to agree on one.

item.title: Writing a product description for an Indian D2C brand
item.description: Most product pages say premium quality and stop. How to answer the doubts a photo can't.
